## Guide: RPAA safeguarding of end-user funds

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-safeguarding-end-user-funds.html

Since September 8, 2025, a payment service provider that holds funds for its users must safeguard them, either in trust in a trust account or in a segregated account backed by insurance or a guarantee. It also needs a written safeguarding framework and an independent review at least every three years.

**Key points:**
- Safeguarding applies only to end-user funds a PSP holds at rest.
- Place held funds in a safeguarding account on receipt. Unavoidable processing constraints allow until the next business day.
- Use a trust account, or a segregated account with insurance or a guarantee, or a mix of both.
- Keep a daily ledger, approve the framework every year and have it reviewed independently every three years.

### Who must safeguard end-user funds

One of the payment functions in the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) is holding funds on behalf of an end user until they're withdrawn by the end user or transferred to another person or entity. A payment service provider (PSP) that performs it must safeguard those funds. The [Bank of Canada's supervisory framework](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/regulatory-oversight/retail-payments/supervisory-framework/) says the requirement came into force on September 8, 2025.

It only covers funds that are held. The Bank's [safeguarding summary](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Safeguarding-of-end-user-funds-At-a-glance.pdf) explains the difference:

- You hold funds when they sit at rest in an account you own, available for a later withdrawal or transfer, and you owe them to the end user.

- Funds are at rest while you have no instruction to transfer them immediately.

- You stop holding funds when you receive an instruction for immediate withdrawal or transfer, or when a future-dated transfer date arrives.

- Funds you receive together with an instruction to transfer them immediately aren't held.

For example, if a user tops up a wallet with you and leaves the balance there for a later payment, you're holding those funds from the moment they reach your account. If a user sends funds with an instruction to pay a recipient straight away, those funds aren't held.

The Bank's [safeguarding guideline](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/safeguarding-end-user-funds.pdf) adds some specific cases. Funds a merchant processor reserves specifically to cover chargebacks or fraud aren't held, and neither are your own funds advanced to a merchant before a card transaction settles. If you have a place of business in Canada, the requirement covers funds you hold for end users anywhere. If you don't, it covers only funds you hold for end users in Canada.

There's one exception. A PSP that is itself a member of a provincial deposit insurance program doesn't need to safeguard end-user funds it holds as deposits insured under that program. It doesn't apply just because the credit union or other institution holding your account is a member. If you're not sure whether your business holds funds at all, our [guide to who the RPAA covers](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-registration-guide.html) explains registration.

### Segregate funds in a safeguarding account

The Bank gives safeguarding two objectives: end users should have reliable access to their funds without delay, and their funds should be protected against loss if the PSP becomes insolvent.

You must keep end-user funds apart from all other funds, including your own, in an account that isn't used for any other purpose. The Bank calls it the safeguarding account. It must be provided by a Canadian financial institution of the kinds the RPAA lists, or by a foreign institution prudentially regulated to standards comparable to Canadian ones. The Bank also expects a written acknowledgement from the account provider that it has no interest in, recourse to or right against the funds for any sum owed to it.

The Bank's [guideline](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/safeguarding-end-user-funds.pdf) expects funds to go into the safeguarding account on receipt. If processing constraints you can't avoid make that impossible, they must be in the account by the end of the next business day at the latest. In that case you must not use the funds for anything else, be able to explain the delay to the Bank, track the funds and tell end users when their funds might not be protected straight away. The Bank treats funds not safeguarded on receipt as a shortfall, so keep a record of them and report them in your annual report.

### Trust account, insurance or guarantee

Subsection 20(1) of the [RPAA](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html) sets out the ways to protect the funds. You can combine them, for example by holding part of the funds in trust and covering the rest with insurance, or by using more than one provider.

| Aspect | In trust in a trust account | Segregated account with insurance or a guarantee |

| How it protects funds | Funds are held in trust for end users | Coverage must equal or exceed the amount in the safeguarding account |

| What the Bank expects | Legal advice that a valid express trust exists, and an agreement with the account provider saying the funds are held in trust | A provider prescribed by the regulations and not affiliated with you, with terms that keep the proceeds out of your estate, payable to end users as soon as feasible and in force after your insolvency |

| Points to watch | Quebec arrangements follow the Civil Code; get advice before paying expenses out of the trust account | Monitor coverage so it never falls below the funds held; notify the Bank at least 30 days before a policy or guarantee is cancelled or ends |

### The written safeguarding framework

A PSP that holds end-user funds must establish, implement and maintain a written framework. The Bank's [safeguarding guideline](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/safeguarding-end-user-funds.pdf) sets out what it must contain at a minimum:

- A ledger that records the funds you hold for each end user, with their name and contact details, and whether the funds are in the safeguarding account. It must be updated each day.

- Your approach to meeting withdrawal and transfer requests. Funds can be held in cash or in secure and liquid assets, meaning assets that can be turned into cash quickly with little or no loss of value. The Bank's list includes guaranteed investment certificates, government securities and promissory notes rated at least A-, and commercial paper and corporate bonds rated at least AA-. It excludes residential mortgage-backed securities and common shares.

- Procedures for returning funds to each end user if you become insolvent, written so that an insolvency professional could follow them using your records.

- An analysis of the legal and operational risks that could stop the framework working, and how you reduce them.

- A review at least once a year, after any change to how you safeguard funds, and after any change likely to have a material effect on it.

Unless the PSP is an individual, the framework must name a senior officer responsible for overseeing safeguarding and for compliance with the requirements. The senior officer, and your board of directors if you have one, must approve the framework at least once a year. The senior officer also approves it after each material change.

### Shortfalls and the three-year independent review

Under the [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html), you must take ongoing measures to find any shortfall, where the funds in trust or covered by insurance or a guarantee add up to less than the funds you hold. Fix a shortfall in a timely manner, investigate its root cause immediately and, as soon as feasible, take measures to stop it happening again. The Bank suggests checking for shortfalls daily as a best practice.

At least once every three years, an independent review must check whether you comply with the safeguarding requirements. The reviewer can be inside or outside your business, but must be suitably skilled and must have had no role in setting up or running the framework or in finding shortfalls. Report the gaps it finds, and what you did about them, to your senior officer.

### Using another PSP's account

The Bank expects you to have a direct relationship with your safeguarding account provider. If you rely on another, unaffiliated PSP for access to an account at a financial institution, the Bank treats that as an indirect arrangement. It won't accept one as compliant unless you can show you've dealt with the trust law, Quebec Civil Code and insolvency problems it creates.

### Where safeguarding shows up in your reporting

Your annual report to the Bank includes information on your safeguarding practices if you hold end-user funds. It must also list each shortfall you found, with the amount, the root cause and the measures you took to prevent it recurring. A change expected to materially affect how you safeguard funds is a significant change, and you must notify the Bank at least five business days before you make it, according to its [supervisory framework](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/regulatory-oversight/retail-payments/supervisory-framework/). Our [RPAA compliance program](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-compliance-program.html) sets up the safeguarding framework with your risk management and incident response frameworks, and PSPs that still need to register can start with our [RPAA registration](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-registration.html) service.

### Questions

**Does every PSP have to safeguard funds under the RPAA?** No. Only PSPs that hold end-user funds at rest, available for later withdrawal or transfer. Funds received with an instruction to transfer them immediately aren't held.

**Can a PSP use both a trust account and insurance?** Yes. The Bank says you can safeguard part of the funds in trust and protect the rest with insurance or a guarantee, and you can use more than one provider.

**How quickly must funds go into the safeguarding account?** On receipt. If processing constraints you can't avoid make that impossible, by the end of the next business day at the latest, and you must tell end users when that can happen.

**How often is the safeguarding framework reviewed?** You review it at least once a year and after any change to how you safeguard funds, and your senior officer, and your board if you have one, approve it at least once a year. An independent review of your compliance is also needed at least once every three years.

**Is RPAA safeguarding the same as FINTRAC compliance?** No. Safeguarding is a Bank of Canada requirement under the RPAA. FINTRAC is a separate regulator, and the Bank's registration application asks for any registrations for retail payment activities you hold with FINTRAC.

Sources: [Bank of Canada, Supervisory framework](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/regulatory-oversight/retail-payments/supervisory-framework/); [Bank of Canada, Guideline on safeguarding end-user funds (December 2024)](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/safeguarding-end-user-funds.pdf); [Bank of Canada, Safeguarding of end-user funds: At a glance](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Safeguarding-of-end-user-funds-At-a-glance.pdf); [Bank of Canada, FAQ on safeguarding end-user funds](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/08/frequently-asked-questions-about-retail-payments-supervision/#safeguarding); [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html); [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html). Checked 16 October 2026.

## Guide: Can you use a virtual office for FINTRAC MSB registration?

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/virtual-office-msb-registration.html

FINTRAC's published guidance doesn't say whether a virtual office is acceptable. It does say what counts as a place of business in Canada, what the registration asks about your addresses, and that FINTRAC can check the information you give it.

**Key points:**
- FINTRAC's guidance doesn't address virtual offices, so no address type is pre-approved or ruled out.
- A physical location, Canadian incorporation, or staff, agents or branches in Canada make you a domestic MSB.
- Your place of business address is published on FINTRAC's public MSB registry.
- A foreign MSB needs a representative for service who resides in Canada. An address can't fill that role.

### The short answer

We checked FINTRAC's pages on registering, on who is a money services business (MSB), on updating a registration and on the public registry. None of them mentions virtual offices, mail-forwarding addresses or shared workspaces. FINTRAC doesn't publish a list of acceptable address types, and it doesn't certify addresses.

So the useful question is narrower: does the address you give FINTRAC describe how your business really operates? The rest of this guide sets out what the law and [FINTRAC's registration page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/reg-ins-eng) ask for, so you can answer that before you file. If you haven't started the application yet, our guide on [how to register an MSB](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html) covers the full process.

### Your address decides which kind of MSB you are

The Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act draws one line. A business with a place of business in Canada that provides money services is an MSB under paragraph 5(h). A business without one, that directs money services at people in Canada and provides them to clients here, is a foreign MSB under paragraph 5(h.1).

[FINTRAC's MSB page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/msb-eng) says you have a place of business in Canada if any of these apply:

- you are incorporated in Canada;

- you have a physical location in Canada; or

- you have employees, agents or branches in Canada.

Two things follow. A company incorporated in Canada is a domestic MSB wherever its staff work. And a foreign business that sets up a physical location here stops being a foreign MSB. FINTRAC's guidance doesn't say whether a rented address with no staff on site counts as a physical location. If you're a foreign business, settle that point before you list a Canadian address anywhere. Our [foreign MSB guide](https://amlcanada.ca/foreign-msb-registration-canada.html) explains the foreign route in full.

### What the registration asks about addresses

Schedule 1 to the [Registration Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-121/FullText.html) lists the information an application must contain. The address-related items are:

| Item | Public identifying information? |

| Address of place of business | Yes |

| Mailing address of the place of business, if different | No |

| Telephone number and website | Yes |

| Whether any money service is provided in a dwelling-house | No |

| Address and telephone number of every agent, mandatary and branch | Yes |

| For a foreign MSB, contact details of the representative for service in Canada | No |

The Regulations make the information in Parts A and C of Schedule 1 public. That includes the place of business address, telephone number, website and the agent and branch details. [FINTRAC's registry](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/reg-eng) shows a business address and website for each listing. FINTRAC's registration page also asks for "detailed information about every location". If you're a corporation, your certificate of incorporation or equivalent record must show the corporation's name, address and directors, so that address should match what you file.

### FINTRAC can check what you tell it

Subsection 54.1(4) of the [Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html) lets FINTRAC verify the information in any registration application. [FINTRAC says](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/respond-eng) it sends a clarification request when information is inconsistent or can't be adequately verified, usually by email to the contact person or the representative for service. You have 30 days to answer. If you don't, FINTRAC may deny the application, or revoke the registration if you're already registered.

Consistency matters more than the type of address. Your incorporation records, bank account details, website, contact details and the address you list should tell the same story. Once you're registered, a change of address must be reported to FINTRAC within 30 days. Our guide to [denied, revoked and expired registrations](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration-refused-revoked.html) covers what happens when these steps are missed.

### Foreign MSBs: the representative for service

A foreign MSB must name a representative for service. Under paragraph 11.12(1)(c.1) of the Act, that's a person who resides in Canada and is authorized to accept notices from FINTRAC on the business's behalf. FINTRAC needs their name, address for service and contact details.

The representative is an individual, so a business address can't serve as one. The representative also doesn't take on your obligations. [FINTRAC states](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/reg-ins-eng) that the foreign MSB, and not its representative, is responsible for meeting the requirements of the Act.

If the representative's name or address for service changes and you don't tell FINTRAC within 30 days, FINTRAC must deny your application or revoke your registration (subsection 11.13(2)). Here the Act gives FINTRAC no discretion.

### Make sure someone reads the mail

The [Administrative Monetary Penalties Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-292/FullText.html) say how FINTRAC can serve documents such as a notice of violation. For an entity, that includes leaving the document at its head office or place of business with a person who appears to be in charge, or sending it by registered mail or courier to the head office or place of business. A document sent by registered mail or courier is deemed served on the tenth day after the date on the postal or courier receipt.

Deadlines in the Act run from service. A notice of violation, for example, gives you 30 days to pay or make representations. If mail sent to your listed address isn't collected and read, those days can pass before anyone in the business knows. Whatever address you use, decide in writing who checks the mail and how quickly it reaches your compliance officer.

### Before you list an address

- Confirm whether you're a domestic or foreign MSB, using FINTRAC's place of business criteria.

- Make sure the address matches your incorporation records, bank details and website.

- Remember the place of business address will be public on the registry.

- If services are provided from a home, say so: the form asks.

- For a foreign MSB, appoint a representative for service who resides in Canada, and diarize the 30-day rule for changes.

- Set up mail handling so FINTRAC notices reach your compliance officer quickly.

We offer a [Canadian business address](https://amlcanada.ca/canadian-address.html) for US$200 per month. Before you use it, we check with you how it fits your FINTRAC registration, and the scope, including mail handling, is agreed in writing. Our [MSB registration service](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration.html) covers the application itself.

### Questions

**Does FINTRAC accept a virtual office for MSB registration?** FINTRAC's published guidance doesn't address virtual offices. It asks for the address of your place of business, can verify what you provide and sends clarification requests when information is inconsistent or can't be verified. The address should reflect how your business actually operates.

**Is my MSB's address made public?** Yes. The place of business address is part of the identifying information FINTRAC publishes on its MSB registry, along with agent and branch details.

**Can a Canadian business address act as a foreign MSB's representative for service?** No. The representative for service is a person who resides in Canada and is authorized to accept FINTRAC's notices. A business address is a separate thing.

**Does a Canadian address turn a foreign MSB into a domestic MSB?** FINTRAC says a physical location in Canada is a place of business, and a business with a place of business in Canada is a domestic MSB. FINTRAC doesn't say whether an address without staff counts, so get this confirmed before you list one.

**Can I register an MSB that operates from home?** The registration asks whether any money service is provided in a dwelling-house, so it's something you disclose. Your address must still match your other records.

Sources: [FINTRAC, Register your MSB or FMSB](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/reg-ins-eng); [FINTRAC, Money services businesses](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/msb-eng); [FINTRAC, Answer clarification requests, update, renew or cancel your registration](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/respond-eng); [FINTRAC, Money Services Business Registry](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/reg-eng); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Registration Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-121/FullText.html); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Administrative Monetary Penalties Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-292/FullText.html). Checked 21 October 2026.

## Guide: MSB registration denied, revoked or expired: what happens and what to do

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration-refused-revoked.html

FINTRAC can deny an MSB application or revoke a registration for a short list of reasons set out in the Act. A registration that isn't renewed expires. Each outcome has its own deadlines, and operating without a valid registration is an offence.

**Key points:**
- Ineligibility revokes a registration automatically, from the day it arises.
- Unanswered 30-day clarification requests can lead to denial or revocation.
- You have 30 days to ask FINTRAC's Director to review a denial or revocation.
- Renew before expiry: a renewal submitted in time keeps you Registered while it's processed.

### The four statuses on FINTRAC's registry

[FINTRAC's MSB registry](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/reg-eng) shows one of four statuses for every business:

| Status | FINTRAC's meaning |

| Registered | Currently registered with FINTRAC |

| Revoked | No longer registered for not answering a clarification request, not providing assistance to FINTRAC, or being found ineligible |

| Expired | Didn't renew its registration after two years |

| Ceased | Told FINTRAC it no longer offers the services |

FINTRAC updates the registry monthly, and a downloadable version is available. It also keeps a separate [list of businesses with revoked registrations](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/revoked-revoquee-eng). Search by name and registration number, and check the expiry date as well as the status.

### Why an application is denied

The [Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html) gives three grounds:

- **Ineligibility.** FINTRAC must deny an applicant listed in subsection 11.11(1) (section 11.16).

- **Unanswered clarification requests.** FINTRAC may deny an application if the applicant doesn't provide requested clarifications within 30 days (section 11.14).

- **A foreign MSB's representative for service.** If the representative's name or address for service changes and FINTRAC isn't told within 30 days, FINTRAC must deny the application (subsection 11.13(2)).

The ineligible group includes people and entities subject to certain sanctions, listed terrorist entities, and those convicted of money laundering, terrorist financing and a range of other offences, including human smuggling and trafficking offences under sections 117 and 118 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Since the Bill C-12 amendments of March 26, 2026, it also includes anyone who still hasn't paid a FINTRAC penalty, with interest, 30 days after all proceedings on the violation have ended. Under the [Registration Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-121/FullText.html), a corporation or other entity is also ineligible if its CEO, president, a director or a 20% owner falls into most of these groups. [FINTRAC's eligibility page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/no-eng) lists the offences in plain language.

### Why a registration is revoked

- **Ineligibility.** If a registered business becomes ineligible, its registration is revoked as of the day that happens (subsection 11.11(2)). FINTRAC then sends written notice without delay. No decision by FINTRAC is needed for the revocation to take effect.

- **Clarification requests.** A registered business must answer FINTRAC's clarification requests within 30 days, or FINTRAC may revoke (section 11.17).

- **Not assisting FINTRAC.** FINTRAC may revoke if a business doesn't give an examiner reasonable assistance, or doesn't provide documents required by a notice served during an examination (section 11.171).

- **A foreign MSB's representative for service.** The same 30-day rule as for applications applies, and revocation is mandatory.

Every decision to deny or revoke must be in writing, with reasons (section 11.18).

### Asking for a review, then appealing

Within 30 days after you receive a denial or revocation, you can apply in writing to FINTRAC's Director for a review and include supporting information (section 11.3). The Director either confirms the decision or substitutes their own, and serves notice with reasons.

If you disagree with the Director's decision, you can appeal to the Federal Court within 30 days after it's served, or within a longer period the Court allows. If the Director doesn't decide within 90 days after receiving your application for review, you can appeal within 30 days after that 90-day period ends (section 11.4).

[FINTRAC's reviews and appeals page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/raa-rea/1-eng) says applications go to its Review and Appeals Unit by mail, or electronically after you email rev-app@fintrac-canafe.gc.ca for a secure link. If a lawyer applies for you, include a letter of authorization. This is general information, and a lawyer can advise on your own case.

### Expiry and renewal

Registration must be renewed every two years (section 11.19). [FINTRAC says](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/respond-eng) it's your responsibility to renew on time, and that most complete applications are processed within three months.

Timing matters because of how the registry treats renewals. If you submit a renewal before the expiry date, you stay Registered until FINTRAC processes it, even if the expiry date passes. If you don't submit one before the expiry date, your registration is treated as Expired.

Virtual currency dealers and foreign MSBs have a specific deadline for their first renewal under section 6.1 of the Registration Regulations. For a corporation, it's the last day of the month of the first anniversary of incorporation that falls after the second anniversary of initial registration. Check the expiry date on your registry listing rather than counting from memory.

### Changes and stopping services

Tell FINTRAC about any change to your registration information, or newly obtained information that should have been in the application, within 30 days of becoming aware of it (subsection 11.13(1)). If you stop offering the services you're registered for, notify FINTRAC within 30 days using its cessation form (section 11.2). FINTRAC says failing to do either may lead to penalties or criminal charges.

### Operating without a valid registration

Section 77.4 of the Act makes it an offence for a business that must register to knowingly engage in an activity it isn't registered for. As the Act reads today, the maximum is a fine of $2,500,000, up to two years less a day in prison, or both, on summary conviction, and a fine of $5,000,000, up to five years in prison, or both, on indictment. Officers and directors who directed, authorized or took part in an offence can also be found guilty (section 78).

The same failures can be handled as administrative violations instead. Under the [penalty regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-292/FullText.html), failing to register, to report changes, to answer clarification requests, to renew or to notify cessation are all serious violations. For violations on or after March 26, 2026, a serious violation can carry up to $4,000,000. FINTRAC can't pursue both a penalty and a prosecution for the same act. Our guide to [FINTRAC penalties](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-penalties-amps.html) explains the process.

There are practical effects too. FINTRAC notes that financial entities must make sure the foreign MSBs they open accounts for are registered with FINTRAC.

### Applying again

The registration sections of the Act don't set a waiting period before a new application. Any ineligibility has to be resolved first, such as an unpaid penalty. The application asks whether you've applied before, so be open about the earlier outcome and what has changed.

Fresh criminal record checks will be needed, issued no more than six months before you apply. Answer every clarification request well within 30 days. Our [MSB registration service](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration.html) prepares and submits applications, and our [registration guide](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html) sets out each step. Some businesses look at [buying a registered MSB](https://amlcanada.ca/buying-an-msb-canada.html) instead, which brings its own checks. If the address on file is part of the problem, see our guide on [virtual offices and MSB registration](https://amlcanada.ca/virtual-office-msb-registration.html).

### Questions

**What happens if my MSB registration expires?** If you didn't submit a renewal before the expiry date, the registry shows the business as Expired and it isn't registered. Providing money services while unregistered can lead to a penalty or prosecution.

**Can I keep operating while my renewal is processed?** Yes, if you submitted the renewal before the expiry date. FINTRAC says the business stays Registered until the renewal is processed.

**How do I challenge a FINTRAC revocation?** Apply in writing to FINTRAC's Director for a review within 30 days of receiving the decision. If you disagree with the Director's decision, you can appeal to the Federal Court within 30 days after it's served.

**Can a business with a revoked registration apply again?** The Act doesn't set a waiting period, but the reason for revocation must be resolved first. An ineligible applicant must be refused.

**How do I check if an MSB is registered?** Search FINTRAC's Money Services Business Registry by name or registration number and check the status and expiry date. FINTRAC says registration isn't an endorsement or a licence.

Sources: [FINTRAC, Answer clarification requests, update, renew or cancel your registration](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/respond-eng); [FINTRAC, Money Services Business Registry](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/reg-eng); [FINTRAC, Money services businesses with revoked registration](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/revoked-revoquee-eng); [FINTRAC, Who is not eligible to register](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/no-eng); [FINTRAC, Reviews and appeals](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/raa-rea/1-eng); [FINTRAC, Register your MSB or FMSB](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/reg-ins-eng); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Registration Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-121/FullText.html); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Administrative Monetary Penalties Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-292/FullText.html). Checked 21 October 2026.

---

## Guide: FINTRAC administrative monetary penalties (AMPs) explained

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-penalties-amps.html

FINTRAC can impose administrative monetary penalties for breaches of the anti-money laundering law. Amendments in force since March 26, 2026 raised the maximum amounts up to 40 times and added compliance agreements and compliance orders.

**Key points:**
- For violations on or after March 26, 2026, the cap is $4 million per violation for a person and $20 million for an entity.
- Each violation is classed as minor, serious or very serious, and the class sets the range.
- You have 30 days to pay or make representations, and paying means accepting the violation.
- Imposed penalties are made public, and a compliance agreement now follows every prescribed violation.

### What an AMP is

An administrative monetary penalty (AMP) is a civil penalty for not complying with the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act and its regulations. FINTRAC has been able to impose them since December 30, 2008. Under the [Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html), penalties are meant to encourage compliance rather than to punish (section 73.11). A violation isn't an offence (section 73.23), and due diligence is a defence (section 73.24).

FINTRAC can also refer non-compliance to law enforcement as a criminal offence. It can't do both for the same act or omission (section 73.12). [FINTRAC's policy](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/2-eng) says that after an assessment it may take no further action, follow up, issue a penalty, or disclose information to law enforcement.

### Penalty amounts in force today

The Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act (Bill C-12) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. It amended the Act and the [Administrative Monetary Penalties Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-292/FullText.html) the same day. The new framework applies to violations committed on or after that day. Violations committed before it stay under the former rules, according to the Act's transitional provisions and [FINTRAC's notice on the changes](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/3-eng).

| Class | Range per violation before March 26, 2026 | Range per violation from March 26, 2026 |

| Minor | $1 to $1,000 | $1 to $40,000 |

| Serious | $1 to $100,000 | $1 to $4,000,000 |

| Very serious | $1 to $100,000 (person); $1 to $500,000 (entity) | $1 to $20,000,000, with a $4,000,000 cap for a person |

Section 73.1 of the Act now caps each prescribed violation at $4,000,000 for a person and $20,000,000 for an entity. The total for all violations on one notice is capped at the greater of $4,000,000 or 3% of a person's gross global income, or the greater of $20,000,000 or 3% of an entity's gross global revenue. For an entity in an affiliated group, the group's revenue is used.

FINTRAC says it scopes each examination so the review period falls entirely under one framework.

### Minor, serious and very serious

The schedule to the penalty regulations classifies each violation. Some examples:

- **Very serious:** failing to report a suspicious transaction; failing to comply with a ministerial directive; failing to keep a compliance program that is reasonably designed, risk-based and effective; and the compliance program elements in section 156 of the Regulations, such as the compliance officer, policies, risk assessment, training and the two-year review.

- **Serious:** MSB registration failures, including not registering, not reporting changes, not answering clarification requests, not renewing and not notifying cessation.

- **Minor:** most record keeping, client identification and threshold reporting items, and the travel rule obligations.

Bill C-12 moved certain compliance program violations from serious to very serious, as [FINTRAC's changes page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/businesses-entreprises/changes-changements-eng) notes. [FINTRAC publishes harm done guides](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/1-eng) for seven groups of violations: compliance program, threshold reports (large cash, electronic funds transfer and casino disbursement), suspicious transaction reports, know your client, record keeping, MSB registration, and other compliance measures.

### How the amount is set

Section 73.11 of the Act lists the criteria: the non-punitive purpose, the harm done by the violation, and, new since March 26, 2026, the ability of the person or entity to pay. The regulations add the history of compliance. If FINTRAC asks for information on your ability to pay, your later representations can generally rely only on what you gave before its deadline (section 73.111).

FINTRAC's published policy works in two steps. First, it assesses harm: how far the violation interferes with the Act's objectives or FINTRAC's mandate, including resulting harm such as unreported transactions caused by a gap in procedures. For a complete failure to meet a requirement, the base penalty is typically the maximum for that violation. Second, it adjusts for compliance history and the non-punitive purpose. FINTRAC says it's updating this policy, with an updated approach to calculating penalties under the new framework.

### From notice of violation to final decision

- **Notice of violation.** It names the violations, the proposed penalty and how it was calculated. FINTRAC must start proceedings within two years after it becomes aware of the subject matter.

- **Pay, or make representations.** You have 30 days after service, or a longer period FINTRAC specifies. Paying means you're deemed to have committed the violation, and proceedings end.

- **No response.** You're deemed to have committed the violation, and FINTRAC imposes the proposed penalty.

- **Director's decision.** If you make written representations, the Director decides on a balance of probabilities and may impose the proposed penalty, a lesser one or none.

- **Federal Court.** For a serious or very serious violation, or a compliance order violation, you can appeal within 30 days after the decision is served. If no decision comes within 90 days after your representations are complete, you can appeal within the following 30 days.

Decisions on minor violations can't be appealed, unless a series of minor violations on one notice counts as serious. The current regulations set that threshold at $400,000 in total. Penalties not paid on time accrue interest and are a debt to the Crown.

### Compliance agreements and compliance orders

After proceedings on a prescribed violation end, FINTRAC must require a compliance agreement (section 73.16). It sets out the measures you'll take and a deadline. FINTRAC can extend the deadline by up to one year if you're making substantial progress. If you don't sign within six months, you're deemed to have refused.

If you refuse, or miss the deadline, the Director must make a compliance order and make it public (section 73.17). The order requires you to publish the measures you're taking. Breaching it is a compliance order violation, capped at the greater of $5,000,000 or 3% of gross global income for a person, and the greater of $30,000,000 or 3% of gross global revenue for an entity.

### Public naming

When a violation is deemed committed, or the Director decides one was committed, FINTRAC must publish the name of the person or entity, the nature of the violation and the penalty amount, and it may include its reasons (section 73.22). Notices stay on [FINTRAC's public notice page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/4-eng) for five years. For an MSB, an unpaid penalty also has a registration effect: 30 days after proceedings end, it makes the business ineligible to register, as our guide to [revoked registrations](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration-refused-revoked.html) explains.

### Lowering your risk

Most violations trace back to gaps an internal check would find. Test your program with a regular [effectiveness review](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-effectiveness-review-checklist.html), fix late or missing reports before FINTRAC calls, and prepare as our [examination guide](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-examination-preparation.html) describes. An [outsourced compliance officer](https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-compliance-officer.html) can keep reporting and records current, and an external [effectiveness review](https://amlcanada.ca/effectiveness-reviews.html) gives an independent view. Payment businesses should also check their [travel rule and directive procedures](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-travel-rule-ministerial-directives.html), since breaching a directive is very serious.

### Questions

**What is the maximum FINTRAC penalty now?** For violations on or after March 26, 2026, up to $4 million per violation for a person and $20 million for an entity. The total on one notice can reach the greater of those amounts or 3% of gross global income or revenue.

**Does paying a FINTRAC penalty mean admitting the violation?** Yes. Under the Act, paying the penalty in a notice of violation means you're deemed to have committed the violation, and the proceedings end.

**Can I appeal a FINTRAC penalty?** First make written representations to FINTRAC's Director within 30 days of the notice. You can then appeal the Director's decision to the Federal Court within 30 days for serious, very serious and compliance order violations.

**Will FINTRAC publish my business's name?** Yes, when a violation is deemed committed or the Director decides one was committed. FINTRAC publishes the name, the nature of the violation and the penalty, and notices stay online for five years.

**Does FINTRAC consider whether a business can afford the penalty?** Since March 26, 2026, the Act lists ability to pay as one of the criteria for setting the amount, along with the harm done and the purpose of encouraging compliance.

Sources: [FINTRAC, Administrative monetary penalties: changes following legislative amendments](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/3-eng); [FINTRAC, Administrative monetary penalties policy](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/2-eng); [FINTRAC, Penalties for non-compliance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/1-eng); [FINTRAC, Public notice of administrative monetary penalties](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/4-eng); [FINTRAC, Reviews and appeals](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/raa-rea/1-eng); [FINTRAC, Modernization and upcoming changes](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/businesses-entreprises/changes-changements-eng); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Administrative Monetary Penalties Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-292/FullText.html). Checked 21 October 2026.

## Guide: The travel rule and ministerial directives: what Canadian MSBs must do

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-travel-rule-ministerial-directives.html

Canada's travel rule requires money services businesses to send originator and beneficiary information with funds and virtual currency transfers, and to check it arrives with transfers they receive. Ministerial directives add stricter measures for transactions connected to Russia, Iran and North Korea.

**Key points:**
- Include names, addresses and account or reference numbers with transfers you send.
- Take reasonable measures to get missing information, then follow written risk-based procedures.
- Three ministerial directives are in force: Russia, Iran and North Korea (DPRK).
- Directive transactions are high risk at any amount, and Iran-connected transactions must all be reported.

### What the travel rule is

The travel rule is the requirement to make sure specific information goes with an electronic funds transfer (EFT) or a virtual currency transfer. It comes from section 9.5 of the [Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html) and sections 124 and 124.1 of the [Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2002-184/FullText.html). [FINTRAC's guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/travel-acheminement/1-eng) applies it to financial entities, money services businesses (MSBs), foreign MSBs and casinos.

Information you receive under the travel rule can't be removed from a transfer. The travel rule isn't a separate record keeping requirement, though following it helps you meet your record keeping and reporting obligations. The EFTs covered are international EFTs, and EFTs within Canada sent as SWIFT MT-103 messages or their equivalent.

### Electronic funds transfers

The rule applies to the EFTs you must keep a record of. For an MSB, section 36 of the Regulations requires records when it initiates an EFT of $1,000 or more, sends an international EFT of $1,000 or more initiated by someone else, or is the final recipient of an international EFT of $1,000 or more. [FINTRAC's record keeping guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/recordkeeping-document/record/msb-eng) has the detail.

When you initiate an EFT, include:

- the name, address and account number or other reference number, if any, of the person or entity who requested the transfer;

- the beneficiary's name and address; and

- if applicable, the beneficiary's account number or other reference number.

When you receive an EFT, as an intermediary or as the final recipient, take reasonable measures to make sure that information is included. If you pass an EFT on, include the information you received or obtained.

### Virtual currency transfers

MSBs keep records when they transfer $1,000 or more in virtual currency at a client's request, or receive $1,000 or more in virtual currency for remittance to a beneficiary. For those transfers, you must send the name, address and account or other reference number, if any, of both the person who requested the transfer and the beneficiary. For transfers you receive, take reasonable measures to make sure the same information is included. Crypto businesses can read this with our guide to [crypto registration with FINTRAC](https://amlcanada.ca/crypto-registration-canada.html).

### When the information is missing

If a transfer arrives without the required information, you must take reasonable measures to obtain it. FINTRAC describes reasonable measures as steps taken to achieve an outcome even if they don't achieve it, such as asking the client, searching open sources, retrieving information you already hold, or consulting commercially available information.

You also need written, risk-based policies and procedures for what happens when those measures fail. FINTRAC says they must cover when you allow, suspend or reject the transfer, and what follow-up measures you take. Write the steps down in your procedures and keep a record of what you did for each case. If the circumstances give you reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering, terrorist financing or sanctions evasion, the usual [suspicious transaction reporting](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/str-dod/str-dod-eng) duty applies as well.

Under the penalty regulations, the travel rule obligations are minor violations. For violations on or after March 26, 2026, a minor violation can carry up to $40,000 each. Our [guide to FINTRAC penalties](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-penalties-amps.html) explains the classes.

### What a ministerial directive is

Part 1.1 of the Act, in force since June 19, 2014, lets the Minister of Finance issue directives requiring reporting entities to apply countermeasures to transactions coming from or going to designated foreign jurisdictions or entities. [FINTRAC's directives page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/obligations/directives-eng) says FINTRAC informs reporting entities when one is issued, that each directive stays in force until revoked, suspended or amended, and that directives are reviewed at least every three years. Every MSB and foreign MSB must comply (section 11.43).

### The three directives in force

| Directive | In force since | Latest change |

| Russia | February 24, 2024 | FINTRAC guidance updated March 22, 2025 |

| Iran | July 25, 2020 | Directive amended February 15, 2024 and November 15, 2025; guidance updated June 23, 2026 |

| North Korea (DPRK) | December 9, 2017 | FINTRAC guidance updated March 22, 2025 |

For any transaction originating from or bound for one of these countries, whatever the amount, each directive requires you to:

- treat it as high risk;

- verify the identity of any person or entity requesting or benefiting from it;

- apply customer due diligence with particular attention to sanctions evasion risk, including the source of funds or virtual currency, the purpose of the transaction, and the beneficial ownership or control of any entity involved; and

- keep a record of it, even below the usual record keeping thresholds.

The Iran and North Korea directives also require policies and procedures to assess the sanctions evasion risk associated with that country. The Iran directive goes further: every Iran-connected transaction must be reported to FINTRAC. Below-threshold EFTs and virtual currency receipts go on the usual EFT or large virtual currency transaction report, marked "IR2020" in the ministerial directive field. Transfers within Canada go on a suspicious transaction report, also marked "IR2020", with the suspicion and action taken sections left blank.

### Deciding whether a transaction is connected

FINTRAC's guidance gives examples of a connection: an origin or destination address in the country, transactions involving the country's government representatives, and use of the Russian ruble or Iranian rial. For Iran, it also lists funds from the sale of an asset in Iran and online transactions traced to an IP address geolocated in Iran. A transfer routed through a third country is caught when details such as the account or third-party information point back to the country.

A client's passport or nationality alone isn't a connection, and neither is a past history of sending funds there, if nothing else about the transaction points to the country.

### Building it into your program

Your policies and procedures should cover the travel rule and the ministerial directives, as [FINTRAC's compliance program guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/compliance-conformite/Guide4/4-eng) expects. They should also say how you learn of new directives and how you decide a transaction is connected. Your risk assessment should record your exposure to these countries. Failing to comply with a directive is a very serious violation, and knowingly contravening one can also be prosecuted under section 74 of the Act. FINTRAC also publishes advisories on countries identified by the Financial Action Task Force. The most recent on its [news page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/new-neuf/1-eng) is dated July 15, 2026.

Our [14-document compliance program](https://amlcanada.ca/compliance-programs.html) includes a Travel Rule Policy and Procedure, and our guide to [compliance program requirements](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-compliance-program-requirements.html) covers the rest. An [outsourced compliance officer](https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-compliance-officer.html) can handle directive reviews and reporting. If you're still registering, check our guide on [addresses and MSB registration](https://amlcanada.ca/virtual-office-msb-registration.html) and what to do if a registration is [denied or revoked](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration-refused-revoked.html).

### Questions

**What is the travel rule in Canada?** It requires financial entities, MSBs, foreign MSBs and casinos to include the requester's and beneficiary's names, addresses and account or reference numbers with electronic funds and virtual currency transfers, and to take reasonable measures to check that information arrives with transfers they receive.

**Does the travel rule apply to crypto in Canada?** Yes. MSBs and foreign MSBs must include travel rule information with virtual currency transfers they're required to keep records of, generally $1,000 or more, and take reasonable measures for transfers they receive.

**What should I do if a transfer arrives without originator information?** Take reasonable measures to obtain it, such as asking the client. If that fails, follow your written risk-based procedures on whether to allow, suspend or reject the transfer, and record your follow-up.

**Which countries do FINTRAC ministerial directives cover?** Three directives are in force: Russia (since February 24, 2024), Iran (since July 25, 2020, amended in 2024 and 2025) and North Korea (since December 9, 2017).

**Do MSBs have to report every transaction connected to Iran?** Yes. Under the Iran directive, every transaction originating from or bound for Iran must be reported to FINTRAC, whatever the amount, using the report types FINTRAC's guidance sets out.

Sources: [FINTRAC, Travel rule for electronic funds and virtual currency transfers](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/travel-acheminement/1-eng); [FINTRAC, Ministerial directives and transaction restrictions](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/obligations/directives-eng); [FINTRAC, Guidance on the Ministerial Directive on Russia](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/obligations/dir-rus-eng); [FINTRAC, Guidance on the Ministerial Directive on Iran](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/obligations/dir-iri-eng); [FINTRAC, Guidance on the Ministerial Directive on the DPRK](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/obligations/dir-dprk-eng); [FINTRAC, Record keeping for MSBs](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/recordkeeping-document/record/msb-eng); [FINTRAC, Compliance program requirements](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/compliance-conformite/Guide4/4-eng); [FINTRAC news](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/new-neuf/1-eng); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2002-184/FullText.html); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Administrative Monetary Penalties Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-292/FullText.html). Checked 21 October 2026.

## Guide: How to get an apostille in Canada (2026 guide)

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-canada-guide.html

Since January 11, 2024, Canadian public documents going to Apostille Convention countries get an apostille. Who issues it depends on where the document was issued or notarized: Global Affairs Canada, or one of five provinces.

**Key points:**
- The Apostille Convention has applied in Canada since January 11, 2024.
- Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan apostille their own documents. Global Affairs Canada handles federal documents and the rest of Canada.
- A document notarized in Alberta, Ontario or Saskatchewan goes to that province, wherever it was issued.
- Global Affairs Canada charges no fee. Provincial fees run from CA$16 to CA$66.50 per document.

### What an apostille does

An apostille is a certificate that confirms the signature and seal of a public official on a document are genuine. Countries that belong to the Apostille Convention accept it without any further step, according to the [Global Affairs Canada glossary](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/glossary). Before the Convention, a Canadian document usually had to be authenticated in Canada and then legalized by the destination country's embassy or consulate. The apostille replaces that chain with a single certificate.

Canada acceded to the Convention on May 12, 2023, and it entered into force for Canada on January 11, 2024, according to the [Hague Conference status table](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-table/?cid=41). An apostille doesn't validate what a document says. It confirms where the document came from.

### Step 1: Confirm what the destination needs

Whether you need an apostille is decided by the law of the country where the document will be used. Canadian law doesn't require it. [Global Affairs Canada](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/faq) and Ontario's Official Documents Services both tell applicants to check with the receiving institution or the destination country's embassy or consulate first. Neither office can advise on what a foreign authority wants.

Ask how recent the document must be, whether a certified copy is acceptable and whether any translation also needs an apostille. Quebec advises applicants to make sure the issue date meets the requesting entity's requirements and to use recent documents where possible.

### Step 2: Find the right authority

Canada has six competent authorities: the federal government and five provinces. The [Global Affairs Canada requirements](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/requirements) split the work like this:

| Where the document comes from | Who issues the apostille |

| Government of Canada (federal documents) | Global Affairs Canada |

| Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Northwest Territories, Nova Scotia, Nunavut, Prince Edward Island, Yukon | Global Affairs Canada, for documents issued or notarized there |

| Alberta, Ontario, Saskatchewan | The province, for documents issued there and for any document notarized there |

| British Columbia, Quebec | The province, for documents issued there; a notarized document qualifies only if the original was issued in the province |

Global Affairs Canada's online [eligibility tool](https://apostille-gac.powerappsportals.com/en/search-document/) tells you where to send a given document. Quebec says it doesn't apostille documents issued by a federal authority, a territory or another province. Global Affairs Canada also notes that some countries accept only its authentication, so confirm the destination accepts a provincial apostille.

### Step 3: Notarize the document if needed

Government-issued originals with an original signature or seal can often be apostilled directly. Private documents, and many business records, must be notarized first. Plain photocopies can't be authenticated, but Global Affairs Canada may accept a copy certified by a notary. It also says commissioners for oaths generally aren't authorized to certify copies.

When a notary signs a document for authentication, [Global Affairs Canada](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/requirements) expects the notary to:

- have a valid certificate of appointment;

- sign by hand in ink;

- apply a stamp or seal showing their full name and the province or territory of appointment;

- state the type of notarial act and the date;

- show when their appointment expires, if it does.

Provincial rules add to this. In Ontario the notary must be physically present, and the [Ministry of the Attorney General](https://www.ontario.ca/page/information-notaries-public-ontario) says documents notarized remotely won't be authenticated or apostilled. Ontario also needs the notary's full signature and seal on the same page. Alberta asks for corporate records and powers of attorney to be notarized by an Alberta notary. Quebec requires an official certificate from a lawyer or notary for private documents, with a signature authentication from the Barreau du Québec or the Chambre des notaires du Québec.

### Step 4: Arrange translations

Global Affairs Canada needs a certified translation for any content not in English or French, sent with the original. The translator must belong to a recognized provincial translation association, or a Canadian notary who speaks both languages must attest the translation. Ontario adds that a document in another language must be issued in Canada, notarized by an Ontario notary and accompanied by a translation.

### Step 5: Submit, pay and wait

Global Affairs Canada takes requests through its online portal. You then mail or courier the documents, or drop them at its distribution centre in Ottawa, which offers no in-person service. Include a prepaid return envelope or label if you want tracking. Ontario accepts mail-in requests at its Toronto office and in-person requests in Toronto, Ottawa, Sault Ste. Marie, Windsor and Thunder Bay. Alberta and British Columbia take documents by mail or courier, and Quebec by mail.

| Authority | Fee | Published processing time |

| Global Affairs Canada | Free | Processing requests received 25 business days earlier, plus mailing time; no expedited service |

| Ontario | CA$16 per notarized document; CA$32 per Ontario government document | Mail-in within 15 business days; in person about 30 minutes if complete |

| British Columbia | CA$20 per document | 2 to 4 weeks, not including mail time |

| Alberta | CA$25 per document | At least 7 to 10 business days |

| Saskatchewan | CA$50 per certificate, signatory or package | Typically 4 to 7 business days, not including mail time |

| Quebec | CA$66.50 per document | Varies with volume; on October 9, 2026 Quebec was processing requests received October 8 |

These are the figures each authority published when we checked on October 21, 2026. Global Affairs Canada also says you don't need to hire a third party to submit a request, and that processing times are the same either way.

### After you receive the apostille

Apostilles from Global Affairs Canada don't expire. Before January 11, 2024, Global Affairs Canada authenticated documents with a red stamp, and a red-stamped document can't be used in a Convention country. You need a new request with a clean version of the document. Global Affairs Canada's [verification tool](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/updates) lets a recipient check apostilles it issued and those issued by Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Ontario runs its own validity check.

### Countries outside the Convention

For a country that hasn't joined the Convention, the document may need legalization at that country's embassy, high commission or consulate after it's authenticated in Canada. Ontario issues a certificate of authentication for those countries. Alberta and Quebec issue an apostille either way, and both say legalization may still be needed. Global Affairs Canada can forward authenticated documents to an embassy or high commission in Ottawa on request.

If your documents are corporate records for a foreign bank or regulator, our guide to [apostilling Canadian corporate documents](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-corporate-documents-canada.html) covers which ones need notarizing. Our [apostille and notarization service](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-notarization-canada.html) coordinates the process for corporate documents, with notarization by a licensed Ontario partner notary.

### Questions

**Who issues apostilles in Canada?** Global Affairs Canada issues them for federal documents and for documents from Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and the three territories. Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan issue them for their own documents.

**How much does an apostille cost in Canada?** Global Affairs Canada charges no fee. Ontario charges CA$16 per notarized document and CA$32 per Ontario government document, British Columbia CA$20, Alberta CA$25, Saskatchewan CA$50 per certificate, signatory or package, and Quebec CA$66.50 per document.

**How long does an apostille take?** It depends on the authority. On October 21, 2026, Global Affairs Canada was processing requests received 25 business days earlier, plus mailing time. Ontario processes mail-in requests within 15 business days.

**Can I get an apostille on a photocopy?** Not on a plain photocopy. Global Affairs Canada may authenticate a copy certified by a notary, depending on the document.

**Does an apostille work in every country?** Only in countries that belong to the Apostille Convention. Other countries may require legalization at their embassy or consulate after the document is authenticated in Canada.

Sources: [Global Affairs Canada, Authentication of documents](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication); [Requirements](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/requirements); [Frequently asked questions](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/faq); [Glossary](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/glossary); [Notices and updates](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/updates); [Document eligibility tool](https://apostille-gac.powerappsportals.com/en/search-document/); [HCCH, Apostille Convention status table](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-table/?cid=41); [Ontario, Authenticate a document for use outside Canada](https://www.ontario.ca/page/authenticate-document-use-outside-canada); [Ontario, Information for notaries public](https://www.ontario.ca/page/information-notaries-public-ontario); [British Columbia, Document authentication fee](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/governments/government-id/guide-to-the-authentication-of-documents/fees); [Alberta, Documents for other jurisdictions or countries](https://www.alberta.ca/document-authentication-other-jurisdictions-countries); [Saskatchewan, Authenticating notarized documents](https://www.saskatchewan.ca/government/notarized-documents-legislation-maps/authenticating-notarized-documents); [Quebec, About apostille](https://www.quebec.ca/en/justice-and-civil-status/services/apostille/about); [Quebec, Applying for an apostille](https://www.quebec.ca/en/justice-and-civil-status/services/apostille/applying). Checked 21 October 2026.

## Guide: Apostilling Canadian corporate documents for foreign banks and regulators

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-corporate-documents-canada.html

Foreign banks, payment partners and regulators often want Canadian corporate documents with an apostille. Some government certificates can go straight to the authority. Most corporate records must be notarized first.

**Key points:**
- Get the receiving party's document list in writing before ordering anything.
- Global Affairs Canada says business and corporate records must be notarized, apart from Corporations Canada certificates of incorporation with an original signature or seal.
- Ontario apostilles business registry documents issued since 1991 without notarization.
- A copy notarized in Ontario goes to Ontario's Official Documents Services, even if the original is a federal document.

### Start with the receiving party's list

Each bank, payment partner and regulator sets its own requirements, and the destination country's law decides whether an apostille is needed at all. Global Affairs Canada and Ontario both say they can't advise on what a foreign authority wants. Ask the receiving party to confirm in writing:

- which documents it needs, by name;

- how recent each must be;

- whether it accepts certified or notarized copies;

- whether translations must be apostilled as well;

- whether the country is a member of the Apostille Convention.

Our general guide to [getting an apostille in Canada](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-canada-guide.html) covers the steps, authorities and fees for any document.

### Federal corporations: Corporations Canada documents

Documents issued by the Government of Canada go to Global Affairs Canada. Its [document eligibility tool](https://apostille-gac.powerappsportals.com/en/search-document/) treats corporate documents differently by type:

- **Certificate of incorporation.** A Corporations Canada certificate with an original signature or seal doesn't need notarizing. One without an original signature or seal must be notarized.

- **Certificates of compliance, existence and amendment, and articles of incorporation.** The tool says business or corporate records must be notarized.

Where notarization is needed, the notary's province decides the route. [Global Affairs Canada](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/requirements) says a document notarized in Alberta, Ontario or Saskatchewan goes to that province, wherever it was issued. A federal certificate copied and notarized by an Ontario notary is apostilled by Ontario's Official Documents Services, at CA$16 per notarized document.

### Ontario corporations: Ontario Business Registry documents

Ontario's [Official Documents Services](https://www.ontario.ca/page/authenticate-document-use-outside-canada) accepts business registry documents issued since 1991 by the Business and Personal Property Branch or the Ontario Business Registry without notarization. Ontario charges CA$32 to authenticate an Ontario government official document.

The [Ontario Business Registry](https://www.ontario.ca/page/cost-time-required-to-register-change-search-for-business-name-corporation-not-for-profit) sells a certificate of status online for CA$26, available immediately, and copies of filed documents for CA$3 each. Ontario's guidance says it checks signatures and seals against its records and needs a hard copy; it won't authenticate electronic copies. Confirm with the eligibility portal that the version you order qualifies.

### Companies registered in other provinces

British Columbia apostilles original documents from B.C. Registries and Online Services, such as a Notice of Articles, incorporation certificate, certificate of good standing and certified true copy. [British Columbia](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/governments/government-id/guide-to-the-authentication-of-documents/process/registries-online-docs) requires notarization if the document has no Registrar's signature, or has no raised seal and you can't provide the online receipt. Alberta asks for corporate records to be notarized by an Alberta notary before it issues an apostille. Quebec apostilles documents issued in Quebec, including authentic acts such as notarized documents.

### Minute book extracts, registers and resolutions

Your company's own records, such as register extracts, minute book pages and director or shareholder resolutions, are private documents. Global Affairs Canada's tool says business or corporate records, including corporate bylaws, must be notarized. Corporate powers of attorney fall under private legal documents, which must also be notarized.

Under Ontario's Notaries Act, a notary can witness and attest the signing of a document and certify a true copy, according to the [Ministry of the Attorney General](https://www.ontario.ca/page/information-notaries-public-ontario). The notary must be physically present, as remote notarization isn't permitted, and Ontario won't apostille a remotely notarized document. Ontario also needs the notary's signature and seal on the same page, and a name and seal that match its records.

### Evidence of FINTRAC or Bank of Canada registration

Payment partners often ask an MSB or payment service provider to prove it is registered. FINTRAC's [Money Services Business Registry](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/reg-eng) is public and shows each business's registration number, status and dates. FINTRAC says it doesn't issue licences or certificates of registration. The Bank of Canada keeps a public [registry of payment service providers](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/regulatory-oversight/retail-payments/psp-registry/) and says it doesn't endorse or license them.

Global Affairs Canada's tool says documents from a Government of Canada department or agency that aren't on its list must be notarized. Ask the receiving party what evidence it will accept before anything is prepared. Our guides to [registering an MSB](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html) and [foreign MSB registration](https://amlcanada.ca/foreign-msb-registration-canada.html) explain the registration itself.

### Translations

Some countries want documents translated into their language. Depending on the recipient, you may need an apostille on the original only, or on both the original and the translation, as [Quebec](https://www.quebec.ca/en/justice-and-civil-status/services/apostille/about) explains. Ask the receiving party which one it needs. For documents going into the Canadian process, Global Affairs Canada needs a certified translation of any content that isn't in English or French.

### Quick reference: where each document goes

This table covers federal and Ontario corporations, and assumes any notarization is done by an Ontario notary, as with our partner notary. Fees are the government fees published on October 21, 2026.

| Document | Notarize first? | Apostille from |

| Corporations Canada certificate of incorporation with an original signature or seal | No | Global Affairs Canada, free |

| Other Corporations Canada documents, such as certificates of compliance, existence or amendment, and articles | Yes | Ontario, CA$16 per notarized document |

| Ontario Business Registry documents issued since 1991, such as a certificate of status | No | Ontario, CA$32 per document |

| Minute book extracts, registers, resolutions and bylaws | Yes | Ontario, CA$16 per notarized document |

| Corporate power of attorney | Yes | Ontario, CA$16 per notarized document |

Global Affairs Canada sends documents notarized in Alberta, Ontario or Saskatchewan to that province, which is why a notarized federal document lands with Ontario in this table. Always run the specific document through the [eligibility tool](https://apostille-gac.powerappsportals.com/en/search-document/) or the province's guidance, because the version you hold matters.

### Common reasons documents come back

The authorities list these reasons on their official pages:

- a plain photocopy, with no original signature or seal;

- an electronic copy (Ontario needs a hard copy, and Global Affairs Canada needs paper);

- a document commissioned by a commissioner for taking affidavits, which Ontario won't authenticate;

- a document notarized remotely, in Ontario;

- a notary's signature and seal on different pages, or a seal that doesn't match the authority's records;

- glued or laminated documents, which Global Affairs Canada can't authenticate;

- a document sent to the wrong competent authority;

- a missing fee or incomplete request form.

Our [apostille and notarization service](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-notarization-canada.html) checks each corporate document against these rules before it is notarized by our licensed Ontario partner notary and submitted. If you're still setting up, start with [company incorporation](https://amlcanada.ca/incorporation-canada.html).

### Questions

**Can a certificate of status be apostilled without notarization?** In Ontario, yes. Ontario's Official Documents Services accepts business registry documents issued since 1991 without notarization. Global Affairs Canada says federal certificates of compliance and existence must be notarized.

**Do minute book extracts and resolutions need notarizing?** Yes. Global Affairs Canada says business or corporate records must be notarized before authentication.

**Does FINTRAC issue a registration certificate?** No. FINTRAC says it doesn't issue licences or certificates of registration. Registration details appear in its public Money Services Business Registry.

**Where does a notarized copy of a federal certificate go?** If an Ontario notary notarized it, to Ontario's Official Documents Services. Global Affairs Canada says documents notarized in Alberta, Ontario or Saskatchewan go to that province.

**Can corporate documents be notarized remotely in Ontario?** No. Ontario's Notaries Act doesn't permit remote notarization, and Ontario won't apostille documents notarized remotely.

Sources: [Global Affairs Canada, Requirements](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/requirements); [Document eligibility tool](https://apostille-gac.powerappsportals.com/en/search-document/); [Frequently asked questions](https://international.canada.ca/en/global-affairs/services/document-authentication/faq); [Ontario, Authenticate a document for use outside Canada](https://www.ontario.ca/page/authenticate-document-use-outside-canada); [Ontario, Information for notaries public](https://www.ontario.ca/page/information-notaries-public-ontario); [Ontario Business Registry fees](https://www.ontario.ca/page/cost-time-required-to-register-change-search-for-business-name-corporation-not-for-profit); [British Columbia, Registries documents](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/governments/government-id/guide-to-the-authentication-of-documents/process/registries-online-docs); [Alberta, Documents for other jurisdictions or countries](https://www.alberta.ca/document-authentication-other-jurisdictions-countries); [Quebec, About apostille](https://www.quebec.ca/en/justice-and-civil-status/services/apostille/about); [FINTRAC, Money Services Business Registry](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/reg-eng); [Bank of Canada, Registry of PSPs](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/regulatory-oversight/retail-payments/psp-registry/). Checked 21 October 2026.
