## Guide: Who must register as a PSP under the RPAA?

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/who-must-register-psp-rpaa.html

You must register with the Bank of Canada if you perform a payment function as a business in its own right, for electronic transfers in Canadian or foreign currency, with a link to Canada, and no exclusion applies. This guide shows how the Bank applies each part of that test to real business models.

**Key points:**
- Register if you perform a payment function as a distinct business, for fiat transfers, with a link to Canada, and no exclusion applies.
- You can be a PSP without holding funds. Storing a customer's details for future transfers can be enough.
- Payments are incidental only when they exist to support another business. Separate fees, user expectations and payment marketing point the other way.
- Agents of a registered PSP are covered by it. Third-party providers and agents of excluded banks are not.

### The four-part test

The Bank of Canada's supervisory policy, [Criteria for registering payment service providers](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/criteria-for-registering-payment-service-providers/) (last updated June 29, 2026), sets out a four-part test. You must register if all four parts are true:

- You perform at least one of the five payment functions as a service or business activity that isn't incidental to another service or business activity. That makes you a payment service provider (PSP).

- The payment function relates to an electronic funds transfer (EFT) in Canadian dollars, a foreign currency or a unit that meets prescribed criteria. That makes it a retail payment activity. Cash isn't an EFT.

- You have a place of business in Canada, or you direct retail payment activities at people or entities in Canada and perform them for end users here.

- Neither you nor the activity is excluded.

Registration must be in place before you perform any retail payment activities ([RPAA](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html) section 23). The Bank's [FAQ](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/08/frequently-asked-questions-about-retail-payments-supervision/) says every PSP in scope must register for itself, regardless of size or revenue.

### How the Bank reads the five payment functions

Section 2 of the Act lists the payment functions. The Bank's policy explains how it reads each one, and some reach further than businesses expect:

- **Providing or maintaining an account.** Storing personal or financial information about an identifiable end user for future EFTs counts. You don't need to hold any funds. Collecting data for a single transaction usually doesn't count.

- **Holding funds.** Funds are held when they're at rest, available for later withdrawal or transfer, and owed to the end user. Funds in transit aren't held. If you do hold funds, our [safeguarding guide](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-safeguarding-end-user-funds.html) explains what follows.

- **Initiating an EFT.** You initiate a transfer when you create the first payment instruction by capturing and packaging the payer's or payee's data. This covers push and pull payments.

- **Authorizing or transmitting instructions.** This includes enabling consent, confirming funds are available, and providing the platforms or interfaces that carry payment instructions.

- **Clearing or settlement.** Clearing includes netting and calculating positions before settlement. Settlement includes posting debits and credits. Software used only for a merchant's accounting or reporting usually doesn't count.

An end user is the payer or payee, who may not be your direct customer when several PSPs are involved.

### The incidental test

A business that performs payment functions only to support another business isn't a PSP. The Act builds this into the PSP definition, and section 3 of the [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html) excludes an incidental retail payment activity unless the other business itself consists of performing a payment function.

The Bank's policy says payment functions may be incidental if they exist only to support your non-payment services or improve the customer's experience of them. You're more likely to be a PSP if payments are a distinct business, especially when you facilitate payments between other buyers and sellers. The Bank weighs three indicators:

- revenue or commercial advantage, including indirect benefits such as data that could later be monetized;

- whether end users reasonably expect to receive a payment service;

- marketing and branding that promote payments.

The Bank's [merchant scenarios](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2023/12/case-scenarios-about-merchants-and-the-incidental-payment-function/) show where the line falls. An online boot retailer that stores a customer's name and address to speed up checkout maintains an account, but the function is incidental and it doesn't register. If the same retailer lets unaffiliated merchants accept payments through its app for a fee on each transaction, payments become a business line of their own and the retailer must register. The Bank expects businesses to reassess as they change.

### How the test applies to common business models

The Bank's fictional case scenarios are illustrative and aren't legal advice, but they show how it reasons. A selection:

| Business model | Bank's conclusion | Why |

| Payment gateway that captures card data and relays it to a processor, for a fee per transaction | PSP | It initiates EFTs and transmits instructions. Handling funds isn't required (gateway scenarios) |

| Website builder whose checkout redirects to another provider's page | Not a PSP | No payment function. Adding its own paid gateway would make it a PSP |

| Money transfer operator that sends funds abroad straight away | PSP | It stores customer data, initiates EFTs and transmits instructions (remittance scenarios) |

| Remittance firm that also offers a multi-currency wallet | PSP | It also holds funds, so the safeguarding rules apply |

| Online marketplace that receives sale proceeds in an account it owns or controls | PSP | Even if another PSP handles part of the process. If funds never pass through its account, it generally isn't a PSP (marketplace policy) |

| Exchange dealing only in cryptocurrency | Not a PSP | No transfer in Canadian or foreign currency takes place (crypto scenarios) |

| Crypto exchange that also holds fiat for trading and is subject to securities law | Doesn't need to register | Payments are incidental to trading, and the securities exclusions apply |

| Crypto-backed prepaid card that earns interchange fees | PSP | The card is a separate revenue stream |

| Counter that exchanges currency for cash only | Not a PSP | No EFT is involved |

### Place of business and foreign PSPs

The Bank treats you as having a place of business in Canada if you have a physical location here, including a home office, are incorporated here, or have employees, agents or mandataries here.

A PSP with no place of business in Canada is still covered if it performs retail payment activities for end users in Canada and directs those activities at Canada (RPAA section 5). To locate end users, the Bank looks at factors such as IP address, shipping or service address and whether the product is localized for Canada. Signs of directing activities at Canada include marketing aimed at Canadians, a .ca domain, offering Canadian dollars or Canadian support, and a target market largely in Canada.

Marketing only to test demand doesn't trigger registration, but serving end users here does. In the Bank's [geographic scope scenarios](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2023/12/case-scenarios-about-geographic-scope/), a foreign payment app that reaches Canadian merchants through an agreement with a Canadian PSP must register, and a foreign app's Canadian subsidiary registers in its own right. A foreign applicant also names an agent or mandatary in Canada authorized to accept notices and orders for it (RPAA paragraph 29(1)(o)).

### Exclusions: the details that decide close cases

Our [RPAA overview](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-registration-guide.html) lists the exclusions in sections 6 to 10 of the Act. These points from the Bank's policy settle most close cases:

- **Affiliates of excluded institutions.** Banks, credit unions, insurers and other institutions listed in section 9 are outside the Act. Their affiliates must register unless OSFI or the provincial regulator supervises them on a consolidated basis.

- **Merchant instruments.** Instruments usable only at the issuing merchant or within a specific group of merchants are excluded. Wide-use instruments may not be.

- **Securities transactions.** Payments that give effect to securities transactions are excluded only when performed by an entity regulated, or exempted from regulation, under Canadian securities law. Its other payments may still be in scope.

- **Designated systems.** Payment functions performed using a system designated under the Payment Clearing and Settlement Act are excluded (section 7). Functions you perform outside the system are not.

- **Internal transactions.** Transfers between affiliated entities are excluded only when no other PSP is involved (section 8). Payments to unaffiliated customers don't qualify, even if they move through an internal ledger.

### Agents, mandataries and third-party providers

Section 10 takes an agent or mandatary of a registered PSP outside the Act while it acts within its authority and appears on the list of agents the PSP gave the Bank. The PSP keeps that list up to date and is liable for violations committed by its employees, agents, mandataries and third-party service providers within the scope of their role (section 87).

The Bank's [agent scenarios](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2023/12/case-scenarios-about-agents-and-mandataries/) draw three lines. A retailer that pays out cash only on behalf of a registered remittance company doesn't register. An agent that also offers payment services to its own customers must register for those services. An agent acting for a bank, which is excluded rather than registered, may have to register itself.

Third-party service providers, which supply a PSP with a payment-related service under contract, aren't excluded. The PSP discloses them and stays responsible for them. Each affiliated PSP in a group also registers separately, even when its parent is registered.

### Before you apply

Run the four parts for each product line and keep a written record. The Bank's [refusal policy](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2025/08/refusal-or-revocation-of-registration-under-the-rpaa/) lists, among its grounds, that the RPAA doesn't apply to the applicant. Many businesses that register with the Bank also need FINTRAC registration. Our guide to [RPAA vs FINTRAC MSB registration](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-vs-fintrac-msb-registration.html) explains how the two fit together, and our [RPAA registration service](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-registration.html) starts with this scoping work before preparing the application.

### Questions

**Do I need to register with the Bank of Canada if I don't hold customer funds?** Possibly. Holding funds is only one of the five payment functions. A payment gateway that captures card data and relays it to a processor is a PSP in the Bank's own example, even though it never handles funds.

**Do crypto exchanges need to register under the RPAA?** It depends on the model. In the Bank's examples, an exchange dealing only in cryptocurrency doesn't register, and neither does one whose fiat functions are incidental to trading and covered by the securities exclusions. A crypto-backed prepaid card that earns interchange fees is a PSP.

**Does an online marketplace need to register as a PSP?** Under the Bank's December 2025 policy, a marketplace that receives sale proceeds in an account it owns or controls is a PSP, even if it uses another PSP for part of the process. A marketplace whose funds never pass through its own account generally isn't.

**Do foreign payment companies have to register with the Bank of Canada?** Yes, if they perform retail payment activities for end users in Canada and direct those activities at Canada. Marketing only to test demand doesn't trigger registration, but serving Canadian end users does.

**Is there a minimum size or revenue for RPAA registration?** No. The Bank's FAQ says every PSP in scope must register for itself, regardless of size and whether or not the business generates revenue.

Sources: [Bank of Canada, Criteria for registering payment service providers](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/criteria-for-registering-payment-service-providers/); [Bank of Canada, Supervisory policy for online marketplaces](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2025/12/supervisory-policy-for-online-marketplaces/); [Case scenarios: e-commerce web building tools and payment gateways](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/08/case-scenarios-about-e-commerce-web-building-tools-and-payment-gateways/); [Case scenarios: remittance service providers](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/08/case-scenarios-about-remittance-service-providers/); [Case scenarios: services backed by cryptocurrencies](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/10/case-scenarios-about-providers-of-services-backed-by-cryptocurrencies/); [Case scenarios: merchants and the incidental payment function](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2023/12/case-scenarios-about-merchants-and-the-incidental-payment-function/); [Case scenarios: agents and mandataries](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2023/12/case-scenarios-about-agents-and-mandataries/); [Case scenarios: geographic scope](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2023/12/case-scenarios-about-geographic-scope/); [Refusal or revocation of registration under the RPAA](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2025/08/refusal-or-revocation-of-registration-under-the-rpaa/); [Retail payments supervision FAQ](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/08/frequently-asked-questions-about-retail-payments-supervision/); [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html); [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html). Checked 21 October 2026.

## Guide: The RPAA annual report for payment service providers

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-annual-report.html

Every payment service provider that performs retail payment activities in a calendar year must file an annual report with the Bank of Canada by March 31 of the following year. It covers your risk management and incident response framework, safeguarding, activity metrics and financial results.

**Key points:**
- File the report in PSP Connect by March 31 for the previous calendar year.
- Financial metrics use your most recent financial year-end. Everything else uses the calendar year.
- The form asks for monthly figures on held funds and transfers, so collect them as the year goes.
- A late report costs $500 a day for up to 30 days, then $15,000 to $1,000,000.

### Who files, and when

Section 21 of the [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html) (RPAA) requires a payment service provider (PSP) that performs retail payment activities to submit an annual report to the Bank of Canada. Under section 18 of the [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html), a PSP that performs retail payment activities in a calendar year must submit the report for that year no later than March 31 of the following year. The report for 2026 is due by March 31, 2027.

The Bank's [FAQ](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/08/frequently-asked-questions-about-retail-payments-supervision/) says the first annual report covered 2025. The Bank makes the form available in PSP Connect ahead of the deadline and, according to its [step-by-step guide](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/How-to-complete-an-annual-report-A-step-by-step-guide.pdf), notifies PSPs when it's ready to complete. If you aren't yet sure whether you're a PSP at all, start with [who must register under the RPAA](https://amlcanada.ca/who-must-register-psp-rpaa.html).

### The reporting period

The reporting year is the calendar year (subsection 19(5) of the regulations). Financial metrics are the exception. The Bank's [annual reporting policy](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/10/annual-reporting/) says you give your most recent figures based on your financial year-end. The guide's example: if your year ends on June 30, you report financial metrics as at June 30, 2026 in the 2026 report, due by March 31, 2027.

Financial metrics are reported in Canadian dollars. If your statements are in another currency, you calculate the Canadian dollar equivalent. You may report unaudited figures if the audit for the year won't be finished before the deadline, or if you don't prepare audited statements for any other purpose.

### What the report contains

Section 19 of the regulations lists the information. In summary:

- **Risk management and incident response framework.** Changes made during the year and plans for maintaining the framework; its objectives, reliability targets and indicators; your operational risks and their causes; how you classified assets and business processes; the controls in place; the resources and roles assigned; how approvals were obtained; training; the reviews, testing and independent reviews carried out; and a description of any incidents.

- **Safeguarding, if you hold end-user funds.** Who provides your safeguarding account and who regulates them; any other PSP through which you use an account; any insurer or guarantor and the terms of cover; how you safeguard funds; your safeguarding framework; each shortfall found during the year with its root cause and the measures taken; and any independent review. Our [safeguarding guide](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-safeguarding-end-user-funds.html) covers these requirements.

- **Size and connections.** The maximum value of end-user funds held at any time; for each month, the average end-of-day value of funds held and the number and value of transfers, broken down by currency and for end users in Canada; the number of end users; and the number of other PSPs you served. A PSP without a place of business in Canada reports the Canadian figures.

- **Other information.** Significant changes made, activities started or stopped, changes in your use of third-party providers and agents, your record-keeping practices, and financial metrics including revenues, gross and operating profit or loss, assets, liabilities and equity.

The current form starts by asking you to confirm or update your registration information. It then has six sections: operational risk and incident management, safeguarding, significant changes and incidents, ubiquity and interconnectedness, financial information, and record-keeping. In the incident section you count every incident in the year by type, including those that weren't material enough to report under section 18.

### How it's filed

You file through PSP Connect, under Reporting, then Annual Reporting. You can save your progress and return later, and the Bank sends a confirmation of receipt once you submit. Its policy says the form may change from year to year, with instructions when the questions change, and the Bank may ask for more information after it reviews your answers. Section 61 of the Act prohibits giving the Bank false or misleading information, and that includes the annual report.

### Late or missing reports

Missing the deadline is a violation. For a violation of section 21, the regulations (section 48) set the penalty at $500 for each day it continues, for up to 30 days. After 30 days the range is $15,000 to $1,000,000. The Bank's [June 2026 reminder](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/reminder-psp-reporting-obligations-under-rpaa/) says PSPs that don't meet reporting requirements may face enforcement action. On June 12, 2026, the Bank [announced](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/bank-canada-begin-publishing-notices-violation-payment-service-providers/) it would start publishing notices of violation and noting them on the PSP's entry in its public registry.

### Other reports during the year

The annual report sits alongside event-driven filings, all made through PSP Connect:

| Report | When it's needed | Timing |

| Incident notice | An incident with a material impact on an end user, another PSP or a designated clearing house (RPAA s.18) | Without delay, and no later than 48 hours after you determine it's material |

| Significant change or new activity | A change that could reasonably be expected to have a material impact on operational risks or safeguarding, or a new retail payment activity (RPAA s.22) | At least five business days before |

| Change to registration information | Changes such as your name, address, structure, agents or third-party providers (RPAA s.59) | Within 30 days after the change |

| Change to prescribed information | Information used for the national security review, such as directors and major shareholders (RPAA s.60) | As soon as feasible, and some changes 30 or 60 days before they take effect |

| Acquisition of control | Someone plans to acquire control of the PSP (RPAA s.24) | A new application, and registration under it, before the acquisition |

One change can trigger more than one filing. The Bank's policy on [reporting changes to registration information](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/reporting-changes-to-registration-information/) gives the example of a PSP that starts holding end-user funds and engages a new third-party provider: it files a significant change notice and a change of registration information. Our guide to [RPAA incident reporting](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-incident-reporting.html) covers incident notices in detail.

### Preparing through the year

Most of the work is collecting information you already produce, in the form the Bank asks for. A few habits make March easier:

- Record held funds and transfer volumes and values each month, split by currency and between end users in Canada and elsewhere.

- Log every incident, material or not, with its type.

- Keep a shortfall log if you hold end-user funds, with the root cause and fix for each one.

- Date your framework approvals. The regulations require your senior officer and board, if you have one, to approve the risk management and incident response framework at least once a year (section 5).

- Keep the record of each review and test. The regulations also require records sufficient to show you comply (section 40).

Our [RPAA compliance program](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-compliance-program.html) includes a framework for the annual report and change notices, and outsourced compliance officer hours can cover preparing the report itself.

### Questions

**When is the RPAA annual report due?** By March 31 of the year after the reporting year. The report for 2026 is due by March 31, 2027.

**What period does the RPAA annual report cover?** The previous calendar year. Financial metrics are the exception: you report them as at your most recent financial year-end.

**Do I have to file if I don't hold end-user funds?** Yes, if you performed retail payment activities during the year. The safeguarding information applies only to PSPs that hold end-user funds.

**What happens if a PSP files its annual report late?** It's a violation. The penalty is $500 a day for up to 30 days, then $15,000 to $1,000,000, and the Bank has said it will publish notices of violation.

**Do the financial figures have to be audited?** No, not in every case. You may report unaudited figures if your audit won't be finished before the deadline or if you don't prepare audited statements for any other purpose.

Sources: [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html); [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html); [Bank of Canada, Annual reporting (supervisory policy)](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/10/annual-reporting/); [Bank of Canada, How to complete an annual report: A step-by-step guide](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/How-to-complete-an-annual-report-A-step-by-step-guide.pdf); [Bank of Canada, Reminder: PSP reporting obligations under the RPAA](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/reminder-psp-reporting-obligations-under-rpaa/); [Bank of Canada, Reporting changes to registration information](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/reporting-changes-to-registration-information/); [Bank of Canada, Publishing notices of violation](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/bank-canada-begin-publishing-notices-violation-payment-service-providers/); [Retail payments supervision FAQ](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/08/frequently-asked-questions-about-retail-payments-supervision/). Checked 21 October 2026.

## Guide: RPAA vs FINTRAC MSB registration: do you need both?

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-vs-fintrac-msb-registration.html

Payment service providers register with the Bank of Canada under the RPAA. Money services businesses register with FINTRAC under the PCMLTFA. Many payment businesses are both, and the two registrations are linked: the Bank shares your application with FINTRAC and can refuse it based on what FINTRAC reports.

**Key points:**
- The RPAA deals with operational risk and safeguarding. The PCMLTFA deals with money laundering and terrorist financing.
- A remittance business is usually both a PSP and an MSB. A crypto-only exchange or a cash currency counter can be an MSB without being a PSP.
- The Bank sends your application details to FINTRAC, and FINTRAC reports back within 30 days.
- If you're an MSB, put the FINTRAC registration in place first or alongside the Bank application.

### Two laws, two regulators

The [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html) (RPAA) gives the Bank of Canada the job of supervising payment service providers (PSPs) to check they comply with the Act. Its focus is operational risk, incident response and the safeguarding of end users' funds. The [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html) (PCMLTFA) is Canada's anti-money laundering law, and FINTRAC supervises the businesses it covers, including money services businesses (MSBs).

The tests are different. You're a PSP because of the payment functions you perform. You're an MSB because of the money services you provide. One business can meet both tests, one test or neither. The Bank's own registration guide says applicants must register with FINTRAC if they are considered an MSB.

### Side-by-side comparison

| Aspect | RPAA (PSP) | FINTRAC (MSB) |

| Regulator | Bank of Canada | FINTRAC |

| Law | Retail Payment Activities Act and its regulations | PCMLTFA and its regulations |

| Who | Businesses that perform payment functions for end users as a distinct business, for electronic transfers in Canadian or foreign currency, with a link to Canada. See who must register as a PSP | Businesses providing foreign exchange dealing, remitting or transmitting funds, transporting currency or negotiable instruments, issuing or redeeming money orders and similar instruments, dealing in virtual currencies, acquirer services for private ATMs, or a prescribed service (PCMLTFA 5(h)), including foreign MSBs serving Canada (5(h.1)) |

| Timing | Registered before performing any retail payment activities (s.23) | Registration required (s.11.1), renewed every two years (s.11.19) |

| Fees | One-time, non-refundable application fee, $2,500 from November 1, 2024, indexed each January | See our MSB registration cost guide |

| Main ongoing obligations | Risk management and incident response framework, incident notices, safeguarding if you hold funds, annual report, change notices | Compliance program (s.9.6), suspicious transaction reports (s.7) and the other FINTRAC reports, record keeping (s.6) and identity verification (s.6.1) |

| Penalties | Up to $1,000,000 for a serious violation and $10,000,000 for a very serious one. Late reports and notices: $500 a day for up to 30 days, then $15,000 to $1,000,000 | Up to $40,000 for a minor violation, $4,000,000 for a serious one and $20,000,000 for a very serious one, subject to caps in s.73.1 of the Act. Failing to register is a serious violation |

The RPAA figures come from section 48 of the [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html). The FINTRAC ranges come from section 5 of the [PCMLTFA Administrative Monetary Penalties Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-292/FullText.html), as amended in 2026. For an individual, the Act caps a single violation at $4,000,000.

### Which business models need both

The Bank's published case scenarios, read with the MSB services listed in the PCMLTFA, show how common models fall:

- **Money transfer and remittance apps.** The Bank treats a money transfer operator as a PSP, and one that also offers a multi-currency wallet holds funds as well ([remittance scenarios](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/08/case-scenarios-about-remittance-service-providers/)). Remitting or transmitting funds is also an MSB service. Expect to need both.

- **Crypto-backed payment cards.** The Bank's [crypto scenarios](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/10/case-scenarios-about-providers-of-services-backed-by-cryptocurrencies/) treat a crypto-backed prepaid card that earns interchange fees as a PSP. Dealing in virtual currencies is an MSB service. Expect to need both.

- **Crypto-only exchanges.** The Bank says an exchange dealing only in cryptocurrency performs no retail payment activity. Dealing in virtual currencies still makes it an MSB. FINTRAC only. Our [crypto registration guide](https://amlcanada.ca/crypto-registration-canada.html) covers that side.

- **Cash currency exchange counters.** The Bank's example of a business exchanging currency for cash isn't a PSP, because no electronic transfer is involved. Foreign exchange dealing is an MSB service. FINTRAC only.

- **Payment gateways and marketplaces.** These can be PSPs without moving money in the way a remitter does. Whether they're also MSBs depends on what they do with funds, so check the FINTRAC side separately.

### How the Bank and FINTRAC share information

The link between the two registrations is written into both Acts:

- The Bank's application asks whether you're registered with FINTRAC (RPAA paragraph 29(1)(l)). Its [step-by-step guide](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/How-to-complete-a-registration-application-a-step-by-step-guide.pdf) asks for your FINTRAC registration number and issue date.

- Once the Bank considers your application complete, it sends FINTRAC your name, address, structure, agents and description of activities (RPAA section 31).

- Within 30 days, FINTRAC must tell the Bank if, in the past five years, you were found guilty of certain PCMLTFA offences or served with a decision or penalty for a serious or very serious violation, or if you aren't registered under the PCMLTFA (PCMLTFA section 53.6).

- After registration, FINTRAC tells the Bank if it revokes your FINTRAC registration or penalizes you for a serious or very serious violation, and it may share other compliance information relevant to the Bank's role (sections 53.6 and 65.03).

On the Bank's side, these are grounds to refuse or revoke. The RPAA lets the Bank refuse an applicant that has such a conviction or penalty, or that isn't registered in accordance with section 11.1 of the PCMLTFA (section 48). The same matters are grounds to revoke an existing registration (section 52). The Bank's [supervisory framework](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/regulatory-oversight/retail-payments/supervisory-framework/) states that it can refuse or revoke registration based on information provided by FINTRAC.

### Order of operations

For a business that needs both, a sensible sequence is:

- **Map your activities against both tests.** List each product and the payment functions and money services it involves.

- **Put your FINTRAC registration in place first, or file both together.** The Bank asks for your FINTRAC number, and FINTRAC reports to the Bank if you aren't registered.

- **Deal with any open FINTRAC issues.** A serious or very serious violation in the past five years is a refusal ground under the RPAA.

- **Prepare the Bank application.** Describe the same business in the same way in both, since the Bank passes your application details to FINTRAC.

- **Keep both registrations current.** Report changes to each regulator on its own timeline, and renew with FINTRAC every two years.

Our [MSB registration](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration.html) and [RPAA registration](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-registration.html) services can be run together, and our guide to [registering an MSB with FINTRAC](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html) covers the FINTRAC application step by step.

### Questions

**What is the difference between a PSP and an MSB in Canada?** A payment service provider performs payment functions and registers with the Bank of Canada under the RPAA. A money services business provides money services, such as remitting funds or dealing in virtual currencies, and registers with FINTRAC under the PCMLTFA. One business can be both.

**Does RPAA registration replace FINTRAC registration?** No. They're separate registrations under separate laws. The Bank asks for your FINTRAC registration details in its application.

**Can the Bank of Canada refuse my application because of FINTRAC?** Yes. The RPAA lets the Bank refuse an applicant that isn't registered under section 11.1 of the PCMLTFA, or that has certain PCMLTFA convictions or serious or very serious violations in the past five years.

**Should I register with FINTRAC or the Bank of Canada first?** If you're an MSB, have the FINTRAC registration in place first or file both together, because the Bank asks for your FINTRAC number and FINTRAC reports to the Bank if you aren't registered.

**Does a crypto exchange need both registrations?** Not always. In the Bank's example, an exchange dealing only in cryptocurrency isn't a PSP, but dealing in virtual currencies makes it an MSB. A crypto-backed payment card is a PSP in the Bank's example.

Sources: [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html); [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html); [PCMLTFA Administrative Monetary Penalties Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-292/FullText.html); [Bank of Canada, Supervisory framework](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/regulatory-oversight/retail-payments/supervisory-framework/); [Bank of Canada, How to complete a registration application](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/How-to-complete-a-registration-application-a-step-by-step-guide.pdf); [Bank of Canada, Registration application fee](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/10/registration-application-fee/); [Case scenarios: remittance service providers](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/08/case-scenarios-about-remittance-service-providers/); [Case scenarios: services backed by cryptocurrencies](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/10/case-scenarios-about-providers-of-services-backed-by-cryptocurrencies/). Checked 21 October 2026.

## Guide: RPAA incident reporting and the 48-hour rule

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-incident-reporting.html

When a payment service provider becomes aware of an incident with a material impact, it must notify the Bank of Canada and the affected end users, payment service providers and clearing houses without delay. The Bank expects the first notice no later than 48 hours after the provider decides the incident is material.

**Key points:**
- Only incidents with a material impact are reported, but every incident must be investigated and documented.
- The 48 hours run from when you determine an incident is material, not from when it started.
- File an initial notice and a final notice in PSP Connect, with interim notices as things develop.
- Notify affected end users directly. A social media post alone isn't enough.

### What the law requires

Section 18 of the [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html) (RPAA) says that if a payment service provider (PSP) becomes aware of an incident that has a material impact on an end user, another PSP or a designated clearing house, it must, without delay, notify that individual or entity and the Bank of Canada. The other PSP doesn't have to be one the RPAA applies to. Sections 11 and 12 of the [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html) set out the form and content of the notices. The Bank can also order a PSP to give follow-up notices (RPAA section 19).

The Bank explains how it expects PSPs to comply in its [Incident notification guideline](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Incident-notification.pdf) (October 2024) and its [step-by-step guide](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/how-complete-incident-step-by-step-guide.pdf) to the notice form (May 2025).

### What counts as an incident

The Act defines an incident as an unplanned event, or series of related events, that results in, or could reasonably be expected to result in, the reduction, deterioration or breakdown of any retail payment activity the PSP performs. The Bank reads this to include any negative impact on the confidentiality, integrity or availability of your retail payment activities, or of the systems, data and information behind them.

Incidents at your agents, mandataries and third-party service providers count, as do incidents they detect. If one of them has a material impact, you report it.

### When an incident has a material impact

Only material incidents are reportable under section 18. The guideline leaves the judgment to you, based on your business model, the services you offer and other relevant factors. It gives examples, which it says aren't exhaustive:

- **Lost funds.** Any amount of an end user's held funds becomes unrecoverably lost or permanently unavailable, for example through theft or a system flaw at the PSP, or because the institution holding the funds fails. Losses caused by the end user's own actions, such as authorized fraud, are not included.

- **Outages.** An outage that materially affects the availability of your retail payment activities, such as one caused by a technology failure, loss of a data centre, hosting or third party, or a cyber attack.

- **Insolvency.** The PSP becomes subject to an insolvency event listed in the regulations.

- **Confidentiality breaches.** Unauthorized access to or disclosure of confidential information that creates a real risk of significant harm, such as financial loss, identity theft, damage to reputation or bodily harm. This covers more than personal information. Weigh how sensitive the information is and how likely it is to be misused.

- **Integrity failures.** A compromised ledger or transaction records, a payee receiving a different amount than the payer sent, funds routed to the wrong account, misdirected instructions, or errors in clearing or settlement.

Incidents that aren't material don't need a section 18 notice. You still have to investigate, respond to and document every incident, and the Bank may ask about them. Your annual report also counts all incidents by type. See our guide to the [RPAA annual report](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-annual-report.html).

### The 48-hour clock

The guideline sets the deadline as without delay, but no later than 48 hours after the PSP determines the incident is material. The Bank's [June 2026 reminder](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/reminder-psp-reporting-obligations-under-rpaa/) repeats it. If an incident starts out below the threshold and gets worse, the 48 hours run from the point you determine it has become material.

The notice form asks separately when the incident started, when it was detected and when you became aware it was material. Record all three as they happen. Build your escalation process so that someone with authority makes the materiality decision promptly, since the duty is to notify without delay.

### Notifying the Bank: initial, interim and final notices

Notices go to the Bank through PSP Connect, under Reporting, then Incident. The guideline describes three kinds:

- **Initial notice**, within the 48 hours, for every material incident.

- **Interim notices**, when there are significant developments or useful updates. You can file more than one.

- **Final notice**, once the incident is resolved and the root cause is known.

If the incident is resolved and you have everything, including the root cause, within the 48 hours, one notice can serve as both initial and final. If your systems are so degraded that you can't file online, the Bank accepts notices by phone in exceptional circumstances.

Under section 11 of the regulations, the notice must give your name and a contact person, a description of the incident and its material impact, and the measures you've taken. The guideline expects dates and times for start, detection, the materiality decision and resolution; how the incident was detected; which retail payment activities were affected; the actual or estimated impact, such as the number of people affected; the impact on systems and data; and the root cause analysis.

### Notifying end users, other PSPs and clearing houses

Section 12 of the regulations requires you to notify each materially affected individual or entity using the most recent contact information they gave you. If you don't have contact details for everyone affected, you post the notice on your website. The guideline expects these notices within the same 48 hours.

- Email, text message or your app are suitable. A post on social media isn't, although you can use social media as well.

- The notice gives your name, a description of the incident with when it began, its impact on the person notified, and any steps they can take, such as changing a password.

- If an incident at PSP A affects PSP B, A notifies B and its own affected users, and B then notifies its users if the incident is material for them.

- If notifying users within 48 hours could increase the risk of harm or the incident, or isn't feasible, tell the Bank through the incident template. The Bank expects this to be rare.

### Privacy law and clearing house rules

A breach that is reportable under privacy law is still reportable to the Bank under the RPAA. You can send affected people a single notice if it meets the requirements of every law that applies. Members of clearing and settlement systems may also have reporting duties under the system's rules. Meeting one set of obligations doesn't satisfy the other, and all material incidents still go to the Bank.

### After the notice

The Bank can order follow-up notices, setting who receives them, when, and what they say. It can also send an information request. Normally you have 15 days to answer, but for an ongoing incident that could have a significant adverse impact on end users, other PSPs or certain clearing houses, the regulations allow only 24 hours (section 43).

The notices depend on your risk management and incident response framework, which must allocate roles for detecting, responding to and recovering from incidents. Our [RPAA compliance program](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-compliance-program.html) includes an incident response framework with escalation steps, a materiality assessment and notice templates. If you hold end-user funds, read it with our [safeguarding guide](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-safeguarding-end-user-funds.html), since lost or inaccessible funds are a material incident.

### Questions

**How long does a PSP have to report an incident to the Bank of Canada?** Without delay, and no later than 48 hours after it determines that the incident has a material impact on an end user, another PSP or a designated clearing house.

**Do all incidents have to be reported under the RPAA?** No. Only incidents with a material impact need a section 18 notice. Every incident must still be investigated, responded to and documented, and all incidents are counted in the annual report.

**How do you submit an RPAA incident notice?** Through PSP Connect, using the Bank's incident notice form. You file an initial notice, interim notices as needed, and a final notice once the incident is resolved and the root cause is known.

**Does a PSP have to tell customers about an incident?** Yes, if they're materially affected. Notify them directly using their latest contact details, or post a notice on your website if you don't have contact details for everyone.

**Do incidents at a third-party provider count?** Yes. Incidents that occur at or are detected by your agents, mandataries or third-party service providers are reportable if they have a material impact.

Sources: [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html); [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html); [Bank of Canada, Incident notification guideline (October 2024)](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Incident-notification.pdf); [Bank of Canada, How to complete an incident notice: A step-by-step guide](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/how-complete-incident-step-by-step-guide.pdf); [Bank of Canada, Reminder: PSP reporting obligations under the RPAA](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/reminder-psp-reporting-obligations-under-rpaa/). Checked 21 October 2026.

## Guide: Ontario vs B.C. MSB registration: which province suits a crypto startup?

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/ontario-vs-bc-msb-registration.html

Today there's no MSB difference between the two provinces. A money services business in Ontario or British Columbia registers with FINTRAC and nobody else, because B.C.'s Money Services Businesses Act has been passed but isn't in force. The difference is coming: B.C. plans to start provincial registration, and Ontario has no equivalent law.

**Key points:**
- For AML purposes, Ontario and B.C. MSBs both register with FINTRAC only, for now.
- B.C.'s Money Services Businesses Act received Royal Assent in 2023 and is still not in force. BCFSA's plan targets 2027/28.
- The B.C. Act names foreign exchange and remittance. Virtual currency isn't named, so regulations will decide whether crypto-only businesses are covered.
- Securities rules for crypto trading platforms follow your clients, so your head office won't keep you out of another province's rules.

### What applies in each province today

Founders often hear that B.C. already makes crypto businesses register twice, once with FINTRAC and once with the province. It doesn't. As of October 2026, [BC Laws](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/23019) shows every operative section of the Money Services Businesses Act as not in force. A crypto MSB with its head office in Vancouver deals with the same AML regulator as one in Toronto.

| Question | Ontario | British Columbia |

| AML registration as an MSB | FINTRAC | FINTRAC |

| Provincial MSB law | None | Money Services Businesses Act, SBC 2023, c. 19. Passed, not in force |

| Who would run provincial registration | Not applicable | BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA) |

| Securities regulator for crypto trading platforms with clients in the province | Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) | British Columbia Securities Commission (BCSC) |

| Expected change | None announced | BCFSA's service plan targets implementation in 2027/28, subject to government direction |

BCFSA and the BCSC are different bodies. BCFSA would administer the new MSB registration. The BCSC is B.C.'s securities regulator and already oversees crypto trading platforms with B.C. clients. For the federal side, see our guide to [crypto registration with FINTRAC](https://amlcanada.ca/crypto-registration-canada.html).

### What B.C.'s Money Services Businesses Act will do

The Act received Royal Assent on May 11, 2023. Section 66 says it comes into force by regulation, and no regulation has done that yet. BCFSA's [2026/27 to 2028/29 service plan](https://bcbudget.gov.bc.ca/2026/sp/pdf/agency/bcfsa.pdf) sets the targets, subject to government direction: finish implementation readiness, including registration, education and compliance components, in 2026/27, then implement the Act in 2027/28.

Once it's in force, the [text of the Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/bills/billsprevious/4th42nd:gov19-3) says:

- **Registration.** A person must not carry on the business of providing money services unless registered or exempt (section 5). Banks, insurers and some other institutions are exempt (section 6).

- **What counts.** "Money services" means foreign exchange dealing, remitting or transmitting funds by any means, issuing or redeeming money orders, traveller's cheques and similar instruments, and any service added by regulation (section 1).

- **Fitness.** The superintendent can refuse an applicant found unfit, for example one that has been refused registration, or had a registration cancelled, under money services or securities legislation in B.C. or another jurisdiction.

- **Investigations.** During an investigation, the superintendent can inspect and copy records at the business's premises and compel people to answer questions.

- **Penalties.** Administrative penalties of up to $100,000 (section 34). Offences carry fines of up to $200,000, and an individual can also face up to 2 years in prison (section 42).

Fees, capital rules, reporting forms and the full list of covered services will be set by regulations that haven't been published. Anyone quoting B.C. capital or bond requirements today is guessing.

### Will B.C. cover crypto businesses?

Not on the face of the Act. Unlike the federal law, which lists dealing in virtual currencies as a money service, B.C.'s definition doesn't mention virtual currency. It can be added by regulation, so a crypto-only business won't know where it stands until the regulations appear.

Many crypto businesses also do things the Act does name. If you convert client funds between Canadian dollars and other currencies, or send fiat payouts, you may be dealing in foreign exchange or remitting funds. Map each product against the B.C. definition as well as the federal one.

Previous trouble also carries over. Because the fitness test looks at refusals and cancellations under securities legislation in any jurisdiction, a crypto firm's record with securities regulators could affect a future B.C. application.

### Securities rules follow your clients

For crypto trading platforms, picking a head office doesn't decide which securities rules apply. Under [CSA Staff Notice 21-332](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/2/21-332/csa-staff-notice-21-332-crypto-asset-trading-platforms-pre-registration-undertakings-changes), a platform operating in Canada is expected to register with the securities regulators, or file a pre-registration undertaking while it seeks registration. If your clients live in Ontario and B.C., both provinces' securities laws are relevant, wherever you're incorporated. Platforms that offer stablecoins are expected to follow [CSA Staff Notice 21-333](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/2/21-333/csa-staff-notice-21-333-crypto-asset-trading-platforms-terms-and-conditions-trading-value).

Firms registering in several provinces don't file a separate application with each. [National Policy 11-204](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/1/11-204/unofficial-consolidation-national-policy-11-204) sets out a process where one principal regulator coordinates the registration. That's a practical reason to think about where your head office sits, but it doesn't take you outside any province's rules.

### How to choose

Since the AML side is the same today, base the decision on the business. Go through these points:

- **Where are your clients?** Securities rules, and possibly B.C.'s MSB Act, depend on where you do business, not only where you're incorporated.

- **Do you touch fiat?** Foreign exchange and remittance are named in the B.C. Act. A B.C. business doing either should plan for BCFSA registration once the regime starts.

- **Are you crypto-only?** Watch for B.C. regulations that could add virtual currency to the definition.

- **Where are your people, banks and investors?** Talent, banking relationships and investor expectations usually matter more than the regulatory gap, which is zero today.

- **Will you serve Quebec?** Quebec already licenses money-services businesses through Revenu Québec, separately from FINTRAC.

An Ontario base may avoid a second provincial registration later, which matters most for a business doing fiat FX or remittance, though how far the B.C. Act reaches businesses outside the province is still unknown. A B.C. base costs nothing extra today. Either way, the work that decides whether you get and keep a FINTRAC registration is the same: an accurate [MSB application](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html) and a [compliance program](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-compliance-program-requirements.html) written for crypto risks. If you're based abroad, our guide to [foreign MSB registration](https://amlcanada.ca/foreign-msb-registration-canada.html) covers that route.

### Questions

**Do I need a BCFSA MSB licence in B.C. today?** No. B.C.'s Money Services Businesses Act was passed in 2023 but isn't in force, so a B.C. money services business currently registers with FINTRAC only.

**When will B.C.'s MSB registration start?** No date has been set by regulation. BCFSA's 2026/27 to 2028/29 service plan targets implementation in 2027/28, subject to government direction.

**Will B.C.'s MSB Act apply to crypto businesses?** The Act doesn't name virtual currency. It covers foreign exchange dealing, remittance and money orders, plus services added by regulation, so crypto-only businesses depend on future regulations. Crypto firms that also handle fiat FX or remittance may be covered.

**Is Ontario better than B.C. for a crypto startup?** For MSB registration there's no difference today: both are FINTRAC-only. Ontario has no plan for provincial MSB registration, while B.C. does, so a business doing fiat FX or remittance avoids a possible second registration in Ontario.

**If my company is in Ontario, can I ignore B.C. rules?** Not for securities. Crypto trading platforms deal with the securities regulators where their clients are. How far B.C.'s MSB Act will reach outside the province will be clearer once it and its regulations are in force.

Sources: [BC Laws, Money Services Businesses Act, SBC 2023, c. 19](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/23019); [Bill 19, Money Services Businesses Act, third reading text](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/bills/billsprevious/4th42nd:gov19-3); [BCFSA 2026/27 to 2028/29 Service Plan](https://bcbudget.gov.bc.ca/2026/sp/pdf/agency/bcfsa.pdf); [FINTRAC, Money services businesses](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/msb-eng); [CSA Staff Notice 21-332](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/2/21-332/csa-staff-notice-21-332-crypto-asset-trading-platforms-pre-registration-undertakings-changes); [CSA Staff Notice 21-333](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/2/21-333/csa-staff-notice-21-333-crypto-asset-trading-platforms-terms-and-conditions-trading-value); [National Policy 11-204, Process for Registration in Multiple Jurisdictions](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/1/11-204/unofficial-consolidation-national-policy-11-204); [Revenu Québec, Money-services business licence](https://www.revenuquebec.ca/en/businesses/sector-specific-measures/money-services-businesses-msbs/money-services-business-licence-application/). Checked 22 October 2026.
